h1: EV Charger Installation in Broward County
intro: A home EV charger is only as safe as the electrical service behind it. The question is not which charger you buy, but whether your panel and service can safely carry a Level 2 charger's heavy, steady load for hours. Our crew checks your service first, tells you plainly what it can handle, and if it needs an upgrade first, we say so once and leave the decision to you.

definition.heading: What is EV charger installation
definition.body: EV charger installation adds a dedicated circuit and unit so an electric vehicle can charge safely at home. A Level 2 home charger runs on a 240 volt circuit and draws a large, steady current for hours. So the real work is not mounting the box; it is confirming the panel, wiring, and service can carry the load without heat or nuisance trips.

symptoms.title: A new EV and a slow trickle at the outlet
symptoms.body: You plugged the car into a regular wall outlet and it barely gained range overnight. A standard outlet was never meant for this; a dedicated charging circuit is what lets you leave each morning fully charged.

symptoms.title: The breaker trips when the car is charging
symptoms.body: You start a charge and a breaker kicks off, or the area goes dark. That is the panel telling you the load is more than the circuit was built to carry, and it needs a proper look before it becomes a hazard.

symptoms.title: The panel is full, or the home predates electric cars
symptoms.body: Every slot in the panel is taken, or the service was sized decades ago for a home that never imagined an EV in the driveway. Either way, the capacity question is real and should be answered before you commit to a charger.

symptoms.title: A warm cord or a discolored outlet
symptoms.body: The charging cord feels hot to the touch, or the outlet has browned around the plug. That is heat where there should be none, and it is a fire risk, so stop using it and have the circuit assessed right away.

localSections.heading: South Florida homes and the panels they were built with
localSections.body: Much of Broward County's housing stock predates the EV, wired for the appliances of the 1960s, 70s, and 80s. Some of those panels are still sound; others are known problem brands. A charger asks the service to do something it was never planned for, so we check the panel and service before we talk about the charger at all.

localSections.heading: Heat, humidity, and salt air are part of the job
localSections.body: Electrical work in South Florida lives with heat, humidity, and coastal salt air, all hard on connections over time. A charging circuit runs warm because it carries a heavy load for hours in an already warm, damp climate. So we account for it with proper conductors, solid terminations, and hardware rated for the location, whether a garage or an exterior run.

guide.title: The honest guide to installing an EV charger at home in South Florida

sections.heading: Start with the service, not the charger
sections.body: People buy the car first and worry about charging second, but the charger is the easy part; what decides whether it is safe is your electrical service. A Level 2 charger pulls a heavy, steady load for hours on top of the air conditioning, water heater, and range, so we assess it first. Sometimes the charger goes right in; sometimes the service needs work first, and we tell you once.

sections.heading: Level 1 and Level 2, in plain language
sections.body: Level 1 is the cord that comes with most cars and plugs into a regular wall outlet; it works but adds only a few miles an hour. Level 2 runs on a 240 volt circuit and charges several times faster, usually filling the car overnight. That is what makes an electric car livable, but it needs a dedicated circuit and enough service capacity, which is why the assessment comes first.

sections.heading: What a proper install actually includes
sections.body: A proper install starts with a dedicated circuit and conductors sized for the steady load, not the smallest wire that passes, because undersized wire runs warm. The breaker is matched to the circuit, connections are solid since loose terminations cause most heat, and the run is protected for its location. A charger pulls hard for hours nightly for years, so the only install worth paying for is built to carry it safely.

faqs.question: Can any home get an EV charger?
faqs.answer: Almost any home can, but not every home as it stands today. It depends on whether your electrical service can safely carry the charger's steady load, which is why we assess the panel and service first. Some homes are ready right away, and some need an upgrade before a charger goes in.

faqs.question: How do I know if my panel can handle a charger?
faqs.answer: You usually cannot know for certain from the outside. It depends on the panel's rating, how full it is, the size of the incoming service, and how much power the home already uses at once. We come out, assess all of it, and give you a clear answer rather than a hopeful guess.

faqs.question: Do I need a permit for an EV charger?
faqs.answer: In most cases, yes. Adding a dedicated 240 volt circuit is electrical work that Broward County building departments expect to see permitted and inspected. We pull the permit in our own name where it is required and meet the inspector in person, so you are not left chasing paperwork.

faqs.question: Do you install EV chargers for commercial properties?
faqs.answer: Yes. We install chargers for both homes and commercial properties across Broward County. Commercial installs raise the same core question about whether the service can carry the added load, just at a larger scale, so we assess the service and give you one honest price the same way we do for a home.
